key_terms.meaning: Movement of a component caused by a concentration difference.
A phase or material that blocks one component more than another, so a separation is possible.
Adding a solvent, gas or other phase that selectively takes up a component.
Making a new phase by heating, cooling or vaporizing so components divide between phases.
An adsorbent, ion-exchange resin or similar solid that selectively holds a component.
Velocity of species i measured relative to the molar-average velocity of the mixture.
Moles of species i crossing unit area per unit time, N_i = c_i u_i.
J_A = -D_AB dC_A/dz for binary diffusion; J_A is diffusion flux relative to the mixture.
∂C_A/∂t = D_AB ∂²C_A/∂z² for constant D, no reaction and one-dimensional diffusion.
N_A = -N_B, so N_A = D_AB (C_A1 - C_A2)/z for a binary gas.
(y_B)lm = (y_B2 - y_B1)/ln(y_B2/y_B1), the factor that corrects stagnant-B diffusion.
Treat a slowly moving boundary as steady at each instant and integrate over time.
D_AB, in m²/s, the property that measures how easily A diffuses through B.
D = D₀ exp(-E_a/(RT)) for solid diffusion, where E_a is activation energy.
Pore diffusion controlled by molecule-wall collisions, with D_K increasing with pore radius and √T.
Multicomponent flux relations in which every pair i-j has its own diffusivity D_ij.
D_i,mixture = (1 - y_i)/Σ(y_j/D_ij), useful for a dilute species i in a multicomponent gas.
Fo_m = D t/L², the dimensionless time used in unsteady diffusion.

takeaways: Every separation operation is a named way of arranging a concentration gradient and a contacting pattern so one component moves faster.
Fick's first law links diffusion flux to the negative concentration gradient; Fick's second law adds conservation of mass to give concentration versus time.
Equimolar counter-diffusion uses the plain mole-fraction difference, while stagnant-B diffusion is larger by the factor 1/(y_B)lm.
When the diffusion area changes, the total rate stays constant but the flux changes, so Fick's law must be integrated over the geometry.
Pseudo-steady treatment works when a boundary moves slowly enough that each instant can be solved as a steady problem.
D is measured in a known geometry or predicted from kinetic theory and group correlations; solid D values are small and rise steeply with temperature.
With three or more species, each flux depends on all gradients, and Stefan–Maxwell or Wilke relations are needed.
Unsteady diffusion answers come as charts, series or error functions, organized by dimensionless groups such as Fo_m.
bank_note: Long answers usually stress classification of operations, the two Fick laws with assumptions, steady stagnant and equimolar derivations, variable-area and pseudo-steady integration, D measurement and prediction, solid and multicomponent diffusion, and unsteady charts.

bank.q: Explain the classification of mass transfer operations using barrier, phase addition, phase creation and solid agent. Give one industrial example of each.
outline: Define mass transfer as movement caused by a concentration difference.
Barrier: membrane or wall that separates by selective passage.
Phase addition: solvent extraction or gas absorption by adding a phase.
Phase creation: distillation or crystallization by making a new phase.
Solid agent: adsorption or ion exchange on a solid.
One correct example for each class.

bank.q: State Fick's first and second laws of diffusion. Define every symbol and list the assumptions used to write the second law in the simple form.
outline: Fick first law: J_A = -D_AB dC_A/dz.
Define J_A, D_AB, C_A and z.
Fick second law: ∂C_A/∂t = D_AB ∂²C_A/∂z².
Assumptions: constant D, no reaction, one-dimensional, dilute binary mixture.
Explain that the second law comes from a mass balance on a thin slab.

bank.q: Compare molecular diffusion and eddy diffusion. Define diffusion velocity and molar flux, and show how the total flux splits into diffusion and bulk-flow parts.
outline: Molecular diffusion: random molecular motion; eddy diffusion: turbulent eddies.
Define species velocity u_i and molar-average velocity u.
Diffusion velocity = u_i - u.
N_i = c_i u_i = J_i + c_i u.
J_i is the diffusion part; c_i u is the bulk-flow part.
Eddy diffusivity is not a fluid property in the same way as D_AB.

bank.q: Derive the steady-state flux for equimolar counter-diffusion and for diffusion of A through stagnant B in a binary gas. Explain why the stagnant-B result has the log-mean factor.
outline: Start from Fick's first law and a steady one-dimensional path.
Equimolar: N_A = -N_B, so N_A = D_AB (C_A1 - C_A2)/z.
Stagnant B: N_B = 0, so N_A = D_AB P (y_A1 - y_A2)/(RT z (y_B)lm).
Define (y_B)lm correctly.
Explain that A must drift through B, adding bulk flow.
Compare the two results.

bank.q: A gas A diffuses through a stagnant film of B of thickness 2 mm. Given D_AB, pressure, temperature and the mole fractions at the two faces, calculate N_A. State units at each step.
outline: Use stagnant-B formula with (y_B)lm.
Convert given pressure and temperature to concentration or use P/RT.
Calculate (y_B)lm correctly.
Substitute z in metres and D in m²/s.
Report N_A in mol/(m²·s).
Check that the answer is larger than the equimolar value.

bank.q: A diffusing path has a cross-section that changes with position, such as a tapered tube. Derive the expression for the total molar rate and show that the flux is not constant.
outline: Write N_A = -D_AB dC_A/dz.
Total rate W_A = N_A A(z) is constant at steady state.
Separate variables and integrate ∫A(z) dz.
Use the correct boundary concentrations.
Show N_A varies as 1/A(z).
Give the result for a specified cone or taper if data are supplied.

bank.q: A liquid level in a narrow tube falls slowly as vapour diffuses through stagnant gas above it. Using pseudo-steady state, derive the time needed for the level to fall by a given distance.
outline: Treat each liquid level as a steady stagnant-B diffusion path.
Write N_A in terms of path length z.
Relate N_A to the rate of fall of the liquid level.
Integrate z dz from initial to final level.
Include gas concentration, D_AB and liquid density or molar volume.
State the pseudo-steady assumption clearly.

bank.q: A dilute species A diffuses through a gas mixture of B, C and D. Given the binary pair diffusivities, use Wilke's equation to estimate the effective diffusivity of A in the mixture.
outline: Write Wilke equation D_A,mix = (1 - y_A)/Σ(y_j/D_Aj).
Use mole fractions on a A-free basis correctly.
Substitute D_AB, D_AC and D_AD.
Calculate the sum and then D_A,mix.
State units and the dilute-A limitation.

bank.q: A slab of thickness L is initially at uniform concentration C₀. Its surface concentration is suddenly changed to C_s. Use the error-function solution or chart to find the time for a given concentration at a given depth.
outline: Identify one-dimensional unsteady diffusion in a slab.
Use (C - C₀)/(C_s - C₀) = erfc(x/(2√(D t))) for a semi-infinite medium, or the finite-slab chart.
Define Fo_m = D t/L².
Solve for t or read Fo_m from the chart.
Check whether semi-infinite or finite-slab assumption is valid.
Report time in seconds.

bank.q: Compare experimental methods for measuring D_AB, such as the Stefan tube, diaphragm cell and unsteady diffusion method. Evaluate their assumptions and sources of error.
outline: Stefan tube: stagnant gas, slow liquid level; simple but convection and temperature errors.
Diaphragm cell: porous barrier, calibration needed; good for liquids.
Unsteady method: concentration versus time in known geometry; needs good analysis.
Common errors: convection, temperature drift, impure materials, uncertain geometry.
Compare accuracy, speed and range of D values.
Choose the method for a stated gas or liquid system.

bank.q: Explain diffusion in solids with reference to carburizing and nitriding of steel, doping of silicon wafers, drying of wood or clay, grain-boundary diffusion and hydrogen through pipeline steel. Why is D small and strongly temperature-dependent?
outline: Solid diffusion: atom hops between fixed sites or moves through pores.
Interstitial and vacancy mechanisms.
Arrhenius law D = D₀ exp(-E_a/(RT)).
Carburizing and nitriding: surface hardening by interstitial diffusion.
Doping silicon: controlled impurity diffusion.
Drying: moisture movement in pores and solid.
Grain-boundary and surface diffusion are faster paths.
Hydrogen in steel: embrittlement and pipeline risk.

bank.q: Analyse what changes when D_AB is not constant but depends on concentration. How does this affect the solution of Fick's second law, and when is the constant-D assumption acceptable?
outline: Fick second law becomes ∂C/∂t = ∂(D ∂C/∂z)/∂z.
Variable D couples concentration and flux.
Solutions need numerical methods or transformed variables.
Constant D is acceptable for dilute or narrow concentration ranges.
Compare with experimental data if available.
Explain effect on predicted time and flux.

bank.q: Evaluate why multicomponent diffusion cannot be treated as independent binary pairs. Discuss the Stefan–Maxwell equations and the limitations of Wilke's formula for a dilute species.
outline: Each pair has D_ij; flux of i depends on all gradients.
Stefan–Maxwell gives coupled driving forces.
Wilke formula is a useful approximation for dilute i.
Limitations: concentrated mixtures, coupled fluxes, non-ideal gases.
Compare with exact multicomponent solution.
State where the approximation is acceptable in design.

bank.q: For a gas mixture to be separated, choose between absorption, adsorption, membrane and distillation routes. Classify each by barrier, phase addition, phase creation or solid agent, and link the choice to the diffusion regime.
outline: Absorption: phase addition of solvent; diffusion through gas and liquid films.
Adsorption: solid agent; pore and surface diffusion.
Membrane: barrier; solution-diffusion or pore flow.
Distillation: phase creation by heating; vapour-liquid diffusion.
Match feed properties, scale and purity to the route.
Mention D values, selectivity and operating conditions.

glossary.def: Change in concentration per unit distance; it drives diffusion.
Moles of a species divided by total moles in the mixture.
Mass of a species divided by total mass of the mixture.
A mixture containing only two species.
Motion of the mixture as a whole, carrying all species with it.
Mass transfer between a flowing fluid and a surface or another phase.
Moles of a species crossing unit area per unit time relative to the mixture velocity.
Moles of a species crossing a fixed plane per unit area per unit time.
The proportionality constant between diffusion flux and concentration gradient.
Condition in which concentration at a fixed point does not change with time.
Condition in which concentration at a fixed point changes with time.
A medium thick enough that the far boundary has no effect during the observed time.
A stated concentration or flux at the surface of the diffusion path.
The concentration field at time zero.
An apparent D for a porous solid that includes porosity and tortuosity effects.
Diffusion through gas-filled or liquid-filled pores in a solid.
Pore diffusion in which molecule-wall collisions dominate over molecule-molecule collisions.
Movement of adsorbed molecules along the wall of a pore.
Faster diffusion along boundaries between grains in a solid.
Small atoms hop between lattice sites without displacing host atoms.
An atom moves into an empty lattice site, so the vacancy moves the other way.
Adding carbon to the surface of steel by diffusion at high temperature.
Adding a controlled impurity to silicon by diffusion to change its electrical behaviour.
A factor greater than one that accounts for the longer crooked path through pores.
The energy barrier that makes solid diffusion rise steeply with temperature.
